_work.title: Seven Alchemy Texts — Lawh al-Dhahab and Six Further Treatises (Princeton Islamic MSS, 17c Arabic)
_work.blurb: A 17th-century Arabic manuscript at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts collection, figgy 05fc8244) comprising seven complete alchemical treatises bound together in a single volume of 190 leaves (388 IIIF canvases). The first and primary treatise is Lawh al-Dhahab (لوح الذهب — The Gold Tablet), followed by six further treatises covering the full range of Jabirian practical alchemy: mercury operations (tadbīr al-zaybaq), sulphur treatments (tadbīr al-kibrīt), calcination of metals (taklīs al-dhahab / al-fiḍḍa / al-naḥs / al-zinj), sublimation, compound preparations, and theory of the balance (al-mīzān). The front matter of the codex is exceptional: it contains a multi-page detailed table of contents indexing operations by page number (fihrist), followed by two formal alchemical jadāwil (quality tables, fols. 4r–4v) — ruled grids that systematize each metal and mineral according to its degrees of the four Galenic qualities (hot/cold/wet/dry), in the tradition of Jabir ibn Hayyan's Mīzān (Balance) theory. The texts explicitly cite Jabir ibn Hayyan, al-Rāzī, Roger Bacon ('Rajār Bākūn'), and Albertus Magnus, reflecting the synthesis of Arabic and Latin alchemical traditions that characterized Ottoman-era scientific manuscripts. A distinctive feature of this MS is that the text throughout all seven treatises is written in a diagonal script orientation — alternating direction lines on each page — a compositional strategy unusual even among Arabic alchemical manuscripts. The opening page of the first treatise includes a 3×3 letter square with the letter pattern ن/و/ا (nūn/wāw/alif) forming a talisman-like grid, alongside ownership annotations. Princeton University Library, Islamic MSS, figgy UUID 05fc8244.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 17th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
_work.creator: anonymous compiler; authorities cited include Jabir ibn Hayyan (8–9c), al-Rāzī (854–925), Roger Bacon (1214–1292), Albertus Magnus (1200–1280)

entries.title: Alchemical Qualities Jadwal — Degrees of the Four Qualities in Metals and Minerals (f. 4r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, ruled grid table
entries.summary: Folio 4 recto of the Princeton seven-alchemy-texts compendium (figgy 05fc8244, 17c Arabic), bearing a formal alchemical qualities table headed 'جدول اوزان كيفيات فلذات وغيره' (Jadwal Awzān Kayfīyāt Fildhāt wa-Ghayrihi — Table of Proportions and Qualities of Metals and Other [Substances]). The table occupies the lower two-thirds of the page as a drawn ruled grid: approximately 10–11 columns (one per substance) with 4 data rows plus a header row, and 4–5 empty rows below indicating the table is designed for further extension. Column headers (reading right to left) name specific metals and minerals including نحس (naḥs — copper), and what appear to be sun (شمس — gold), moon (قمر — silver), zaybaq (زيبق — mercury), kibrīt (كبريت — sulphur), ʿUṭārid (عطارد — Mercury/planet), and other substances. Each data cell contains an Arabic numeral — 1, 2, or 3 — indicating the degree of that quality in that substance. The four row labels (right margin) are the four Galenic qualities: hot (حار), cold (بارد), wet (رطب), dry (يابس) — the fundamental categories of Jabirian balance theory (ʿilm al-mīzān). Above the table, a short supplementary index lists page references for specific sections (74, 75, 81, 82 pages, topics including silver operations and compound preparations). This jadwal form — systematic degree-by-substance tabulation of the four qualities — is the visual/analytical hallmark of Jabirian alchemy, derived from Jabir ibn Hayyan's al-Mīzān (The Balance), which held that all transmutation required precise knowledge and manipulation of a substance's quality-profile. The table enables rapid comparison: copper (naḥs) vs. silver vs. mercury to determine which operations will achieve the desired transmutational shift. The ruled grid drawn entirely in ink, with neat numerals in each cell, occupies the preparatory section of the codex immediately before the text of the seven treatises begins.

entries.title: Alchemical Qualities Jadwal — Sulphur and Its Vapors, Degrees by Quality (f. 4v)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, ruled grid table
entries.summary: Folio 4 verso of the Princeton seven-alchemy-texts compendium (figgy 05fc8244, 17c Arabic), the verso of the metals qualities table (fol. 4r), bearing a companion alchemical jadwal (qualities table) headed 'جدول مقدار كيفيات العلاريت غنبر ها علا ما حقق' — approximately 'Table of Measures of Qualities of [the Substance] and Its Smoke/Vapor as Verified.' The table focuses on sulphur (kibrīt), its derivatives and its vapors/fumes (al-ghunbar — the smoke and emanation produced in alchemical sublimation). Like the metals jadwal on fol. 4r, this table is a drawn ruled grid with approximately 10 columns for specific sulphur variants or preparation stages, and 4 rows for the four Galenic qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry), each cell filled with a degree value (1, 2, or 3). The grid has empty rows below, matching the format of the metals table on the facing page. Below the table, at the bottom of the page, is a brief colophon notation: 'أتفق ورشة ا / ١٩٣' — approximately 'Completed in the workshop/session [of]... / 193.' This may record the number of leaves (190 + 3 flyleaves = 193) or a workshop reference. Together with fol. 4r, these two facing-page jadāwil form a systematic alchemical reference section — a qualities atlas — positioned at the front of the codex for quick consultation during practical work with the seven treatises. Sulphur vapors (ghunbar, also the Arabic root of 'amber') are a critical concern in sublimation alchemy: the Jabirian tradition attributed the generation of metals in the earth to the combination of 'philosophical mercury' and 'philosophical sulphur,' and tracking the quality-degrees of sulphur's vapor phase was essential to understanding and controlling the transmutation process.

entries.title: N-W-A Letter Square — Talisman Grid at Opening of First Treatise (Lawh al-Dhahab) (f. 5r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, letter grid with diagonal text
entries.summary: Folio 5 recto of the Princeton seven-alchemy-texts compendium (figgy 05fc8244, 17c Arabic), the opening page of the first treatise Lawh al-Dhahab (The Gold Tablet). The page is composed of three distinct layers. In the upper right: ownership/library annotations recording later provenance — title references, donor/copyist name ('لاه قاسم بن الفضل' — property of Qasim ibn al-Fadl or similar), and bibliographic notes. In the upper-left portion: a 3×3 ruled grid bearing a repeating letter pattern — four corner cells contain ن (nūn), the four edge-center cells contain و (wāw), and the single center cell contains ا (alif). This ن/و/ا letter square has an abjad value profile: nūn = 50, wāw = 6, alif = 1; the pattern n–w–a (nuwwā) can mean 'kernel/stone' (as in the stone of a fruit), a significant alchemical metaphor for the hidden core of transmutation. Alternatively ن/و/ا may be letter-abbreviations for three alchemical principles or divine names. The number '١٩٣' (193) appears adjacent, possibly recording the leaf count of the volume (190 leaves + 3 flyleaves). In the right and lower portions of the page, the dense diagonal text of the treatise begins — the Lawh al-Dhahab proper — written in the characteristic alternating-diagonal script used throughout this MS. Scattered red-ink rubrications highlight section headings and key terms. This letter grid, positioned at the literal entrance to the text, functions as both a compositional talisman (drawing the abjad power of the letters into the work) and an organizational marker distinguishing the preparatory jadāwil pages (fols. 4r–4v) from the beginning of the treatise content. The combination of letter grid + ownership inscription + colophon note on a single page is characteristic of Islamic scientific MSS in which multiple owners added their marks to the opening recto of the primary text.
